name: The Wild Pear of Lysica Hill

location.address: foot of Lysica Hill, Bošáca, Nové Mesto nad Váhom District

access: Free, open hillside at the foot of Lysica Hill above the Bošácka valley; the tree is described as a landmark for local paragliders and model-aircraft flyers, which implies open recreational ground rather than fenced land. No gate, ticket or access restriction mentioned in any source; not confirmed via OSM tags (Overpass query failed from this environment).
transport: Rural hillside above Bošáca village; nearest town Nové Mesto nad Váhom, roughly 15 minutes by car, same as the other two Bošáca trees. No public transport stop at the tree itself.
story:
Nobody planted Bošáca's third champion tree. A bird did, or the wind: a seed from a cultivated pear somewhere nearby landed on the sunny slope of Lysica Hill and took root on its own. Roughly 150 years later it is a wild pear ten metres tall, with a trunk 195 centimetres round.

That sets it apart from its two famous neighbours in Zabudišová, four kilometres away. The pink pear and the heirloom apple there were planted for their fruit. This one is Pyrus pyraster, the wild species, and big self-seeded pears like it are part of what the White Carpathian landscape around the Bošácka valley looks like: a valley that grew fruit for generations, scattering its own trees across the hills.

On Lysica it has become a landmark for the paragliders and model-aircraft flyers who use the hill. In 2024 the municipality nominated it for Slovakia's Tree of the Year, and it won with 2,298 votes, the village's third national title after the pear in 2015 and the apple in 2017. At the European final in 2025 it placed fifth, with 23,729 votes.

The contest's own account and an independent Slovak news report both give its age as 150 years.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a wild pear about 10 metres tall with a trunk 195 centimetres round. It stands on the open slope at the foot of Lysica Hill, 4 km from Bošáca's two other champion fruit trees in Zabudišová.

name: The Multisecular Chestnut of Audran Square

location.address: Place du Général Audran, La Celle-Saint-Cloud, Yvelines (not Viroflay)

access: Free. Stands as 'the central piece of a square, redeveloped especially to showcase' it (contest page's own wording), Place du Général Audran, a public town square in the La Chataigneraie residential quarter of La Celle-Saint-Cloud. No gate, ticket or restriction mentioned in any of three independent sources.
transport: DAY-TRIP ADDITION, genuinely in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, NOT Viroflay: the tree stands about 295m (a 4-5 minute walk) from Gare de La Celle-Saint-Cloud (Place Jean Mermoz), which is a direct stop on Transilien Line L, about 20-25 minutes from Paris Saint-Lazare with no change. From Viroflay (Rive Droite or Rive Gauche stations), also on Transilien lines through Saint-Cloud, the honest journey is one change at Saint-Cloud onto the La Celle-Saint-Cloud-bound branch of Line L; total journey is roughly 25-30 minutes door to door depending on the timetable, not a direct line. State this as a same-network day trip with one change, never as walking distance from Viroflay.
story:
This chestnut's shape was cut into it by winegrowers. Its branches used to be lopped to make stakes for the vineyards, which is why it grew low, wide and twisted rather than tall, with bark that spirals up the trunk and a crown now eighteen metres across.

It was once a lonely tree in the middle of a meadow. Then the town grew all around it, and La Celle-Saint-Cloud did something towns rarely do for a tree that is in the way: it redesigned a square, Place du Général Audran, specifically to show it off. The chestnut is the centrepiece, in a residential quarter called La Châtaigneraie, the chestnut grove.

The European contest page, French Wikipedia and a Paris news site all give it about 330 years, and Le Parisien reported in 2022 that it went in under Louis XIV. That is an estimate repeated consistently, not a ring count, and nobody has published its girth. If you have measured it, tell us.

In 2021 it was voted Île-de-France's tree of the year, then won France's national public vote, nominated by the heritage-tree association A.R.B.R.E.S. At the European final in 2022 it placed eighth of sixteen, with 28,119 votes.

It does not stand in Viroflay. It stands in La Celle-Saint-Cloud, a five-minute walk from the station, direct on Transilien line L from Paris Saint-Lazare; from Viroflay the trip takes a change at Saint-Cloud.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, wide, twisted crown, about 18 metres across, and the bark spiralling up its trunk. It stands as the centrepiece of Place du Général Audran, five minutes' walk from La Celle-Saint-Cloud station.

best_time.label: October, when the chestnuts ripen in their spiny burs

name: The Tree of Freedom of Waret-la-Chaussée

location.address: Rue de la Croisette, Waret-la-Chaussée, Eghezée, Namur

verified_sources: OpenStreetMap node 6916105158 (natural=tree, name=Arbre de la liberte, denotation=natural_monument), confirmed via Nominatim reverse geocode and the OSM API directly
access: Free. Stands beside Rue de la Croisette, a public road in the village of Waret-la-Chaussee (confirmed by OSM/Nominatim reverse geocode), tagged on OpenStreetMap as an officially denoted natural monument (denotation=natural_monument). No gate, ticket or restriction in any source.
transport: SAME-COMMUNE ADDITION to Liernu (data/cities/liernu.json), not the same village: Waret-la-Chaussee is a separate village of the Eghezee municipality, about 8.5km from Liernu by straight-line distance. No train station in either village, same as Liernu's own entry ('reached by road from Eghezee'). Eghezee's TEC bus line 71 and an on-demand local transport service cover the commune's villages, but no source confirms a fast direct scheduled link between the two specific villages, so this is honestly a road/car connection (roughly 10-15 minutes' drive) rather than a confirmed ~30-minute public-transport day trip; state it as reached by road, the same honest phrasing already used for Liernu itself.
story:
This horse chestnut was planted to celebrate a king's death. In 1796, with the Southern Netherlands under French rule, it went into the ground at Waret-la-Chaussée as an arbre de la liberté, a liberty tree, marking the fall of "the tyrant" Louis XVI. Both the European contest page and the Belgian broadcaster RTBF give that year. The tree's own entry on OpenStreetMap says 1769, which cannot be right, since Louis XVI was not even on the throne until 1774; it is probably 1796 with two digits swapped.

Eleven years later it gained a second meaning. In 1807 a stone niche went up at the tree, a shrine to Saint Joseph, patron of workers and craftsmen, and a revolutionary tree became a devotional one without anybody cutting it down.

It is now 20 to 22 metres tall, depending on who measured, and it was 334 centimetres round in 1997, the last published figure, so it will have put on wood since. It is recorded as a natural monument.

A local association, Pour la ruralité de Waret, nominated it for Belgium's Tree of the Year as a stand for the village's rural character. It won, and represented Belgium at the European final in 2020, placing fifteenth of sixteen with 10,942 votes.

Waret-la-Chaussée is a separate village of Eghezée, 8.5 km from the Gros Chêne of Liernu and reached by road.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stone niche to Saint Joseph set at the tree, a horse chestnut 20 to 22 metres tall and over 3.3 metres round. It stands beside Rue de la Croisette in Waret-la-Chaussée.

best_time.label: May, when white candles stand upright over the whole crown
